draft.title: Technology in operations
card: Automation
machines or software doing tasks with little human input, such as a conveyor line that sorts and packs goods.
Robotics
programmable machines that carry out physical tasks, such as welding car parts. Computer systems run and track operations, such as stock control software.
Used well, these tools speed up production and cut errors, because machines repeat a task the same way each time.
They cost a lot to buy and set up, and they can replace jobs that people did before. A business weighs these costs against the gains.
draft.remember: Technology gives faster production with fewer errors, but it costs a lot to set up and can replace jobs.

a.q: A bakery in Newcastle installs a robot arm that packs loaves into trays. Which result would the bakery most likely expect?
opts: Faster packing with fewer mistakes
Lower set-up costs than hiring workers
More packing jobs for staff
Slower packing but more varied results
a.why: A robot repeats the same task quickly and in the same way, so speed rises and errors fall. Lower set-up costs is tempting, but machines cost a lot to buy and install.
a.clue: Think about what a machine does the same way every time.

b.q: Dev owns a small furniture factory in Orange. He is thinking about buying an automated cutting machine that would replace two of his five workers. Which statement best describes his decision?
opts: Faster, accurate output must be weighed against cost and jobs
Output would rise, so there is no downside to weigh
The machine would be cheap to set up but would slow output
Automation would cut errors but could not affect his staff
b.why: The machine can speed up production and cut errors, but it costs a lot to set up and replaces jobs, so Dev must weigh both sides. The option saying there is no downside is wrong because it ignores set-up cost and job losses.
b.clue: The card says a business weighs the gains against the costs.
